comments.author: Nevermark
comments.text:
I think the dichotomy of open-research vs. commercially-driven innovation might be easier to coordinate, with three stages, not two:
1. Open research: Great creative freedom, with great resource constraints. Lots of ideas, lots of things tried, at insignificant cost relative to commercial work.
2. Results filtering, vetting, regularization: Opportunistic selection of apparently successful work from stage 1, for tentative testing at increasing scale. The best ideas end up with moderate budgets that verify benefits, which are reworked for compatibility before any handoff to stage 3.
3. Commercial efforts: aimed strictly at improving quality and economics of current revenue sources.
Mediating between just #1 and #2 involves too much dissonance over globally complementary but locally incompatible values. #3 can be a relatively small group, but keeps #1 and #2 from butting heads, while facilitating them both.
Without #2, the gap between #1 and #3 is too great.

comments.author: bcherny
comments.text:
Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.
That said, a few thoughts:
1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
)
2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.
3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see
https://github.com/security/plans
)

comments.author: tsergiu
comments.text:
I'm super paranoid about the level of access AI agents have. At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.
The best solution I've been able to come up is using an ephemeral vm (on an isolated network) per task, using --dangerously-skip-permissions so it doesn't bother me. I couple that with an API proxy that lets me restrict the permissions it has to external services. So e.g. where a quickbooks API key gives the holder "god mode" access, the proxy lets the agent do certain read commands without confirmation, but all write endpoints except uploading receipts require confirmation on my phone before they'll be allowed to hit the quickbooks servers. I no longer need to trust that the agent will interpret my readonly wishes correctly.
Tooting my own horn here, but this setup works incredibly well! I've been able to connect dozens of services safely where I absolutely do not trust giving raw, overpowered credentials or oauth integration to the agent directly. I actually just released the API proxy today at
https://keycontain.com

comments.author: thomascountz
comments.text:
At one point in my life, I would've found this data fascinating (if it were opt-in, perhaps)! Now, I find it exhausting.
A similar discussion came up recently with Siri Recap[1], where some expressed how useful they thought it was and that, as a party to the conversations it summarizes, there was very little moral or ethical concern. But I have a social concern.
If I'm having a chat with someone, there's a milieu constructed around the fact that not everything will be remembered verbatim. There are all sorts of social and contextual cues that can easily get lost if listening gets replaced by flat relentless transcription.
With Recaps and this social graph (were it to be productized), the informal fluidity in the way we relate to one another starts to go away, and the expectations that follow from that become artificial and burdensome. In the same way that autocorrect has made typos unacceptable, how could you ever be forgiven for forgetting the name of your colleague's new nephew or the Italian village that your neighbor took a spontaneous boat trip to while on vacation last year?

comments.author: twotwotwo
comments.text:
People often talk about how fast old software is, but one of the things that stands out about GeoWorks for me is how
small
it was while doing a lot.
Of course, lots of things that make modern software bigger are things we very much don't want to do without--full Unicode support, accessibility, clever rendering, improvements to quality of life. But our 'foundations' are also built higher; the Web platform and a bunch of native toolkits provide a lot out of the box. (The platform doesn't include all the widgets that are now quasi-standard, of course, so we build a lot on top anyway.)
There are also a ton of useful third-party libraries you can call on without getting too bloated, and there's a lot that would have been bloated then but not now: in the 90s you probably wouldn't embed an SQL DB you didn't really need, but SQLite is a pretty safe dependency now.
Nothing in particular I'm really driving towards here but I think "how do I keep the code to functionality ratio good" can still be an interesting angle from which to look at high-level design decisions even as a lot of the circumstances and numbers have changed over decades.
